summary: Specifies using the KeyNote trust-management system as an authorization extension in the TLS handshake, following the guidance in RFC 5878. Hello extensions confirm both sides support it before authorization data is exchanged. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: TLS authenticates the two ends of a connection. KeyNote credentials add a second thing: they say which actions each end is allowed to perform. This RFC registers the formats used to carry those credentials during the handshake.

questions: how does keynote work with tls
which tls authorization data types does keynote use
subtitle: How to send KeyNote credentials during a TLS handshake, either inline or by URL.

tldr.problem: TLS authenticates a peer, but a peer may also need to show credentials that authorize it to do certain things.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers two authorization data types, 64 and 65, for the TLS authorization extensions. One carries a list of KeyNote assertions directly and the other carries a URL and hash from which the list is fetched.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational, Independent Submission document, and it has been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 6042 is an Informational RFC from October 2010. It is a contribution to the RFC Series made independently of any other RFC stream, so it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard, and it has been updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: KeyNote Credentials in TLS
sections.content:
This document specifies the use of the KeyNote trust-management system as an authorization extension in the TLS Handshake Protocol, according to the guidelines in RFC 5878. Extensions carried in the client and server hello messages confirm that both parties support the desired authorization data types, and then, if both the client and the server support them, KeyNote credentials are exchanged in the supplemental data handshake message.

The KeyNote credential assertions can authorize the client and/or the server to perform certain actions. In most usage scenarios they are signed by a cryptographic public key, and by using the X.509 key and signature encoding it is possible to add KeyNote-based authorization and policy compliance support to the existing, unmodified X.509 authentication exchange in TLS.

A list of KeyNote credentials, for example one forming a delegation chain, may be sent as part of the same payload, or a URL pointing to the location of such a list may be provided instead. In most scenarios at least one of these credentials is issued to the public key of the transmitter of the credentials, meaning that public key appears in the Licensees field of at least one assertion. The same public key will generally be used by the transmitter to authenticate in the TLS exchange, and the authentication material used for that is handed to the KeyNote evaluation engine as an Action Authorizer.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS lets a client and a server authenticate each other. Authentication alone does not say what a party may do. KeyNote credentials carry that permission, and this RFC describes how to exchange them during the handshake.

sections.title: The Assertion List Type
sections.content:
The first type registered in the TLS Authorization Data Formats registry is keynote_assertion_list(64). When that value is present, the authorization data is a list of KeyNote credential assertions that conforms to the profile in RFC 2704. The list travels inside an AuthorizationDataEntry structure as an opaque sequence of 1 to 2^16-1 bytes.

The field holds an ASCII-encoded list of signed KeyNote assertions, and the assertions are separated by two newline characters. A KeyNote assertion is a structure similar to a public key certificate; the main difference is that instead of a binding between a name and a public key, KeyNote assertions bind public keys to authorization rules, and those rules are evaluated by the peer when the sender later issues specific requests.

Making an authorization decision from a list of assertions needs proper linkage between the assertions and the public key certificate that is transferred in the TLS Certificate message. Receivers of a KeyNote assertion list should initialize the ACTION_AUTHORIZER variable to the sender's public key, the one used to authenticate the TLS exchange. If a different authentication mechanism is used, it is the responsibility of the credential issuer to issue the appropriate credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of credentials is sent as plain text inside one authorization data entry. Each signed assertion is separated by two newline characters. A KeyNote assertion binds a public key to rules about what that key may do, rather than to a name.

sections.title: The Assertion List URL Type
sections.content:
The second type is keynote_assertion_list_url(65). A KeyNote Assertion List URL is transmitted inside an AuthorizationDataEntry structure as a URLandHash structure. When that value is present, the authorization data is the same kind of list of KeyNote assertions, except that the list is fetched with the supplied URL. A one-way hash value is provided so that the intended assertion list is obtained.

Implementations that support this type MUST support URLs that employ the HTTP scheme, and they MUST confirm that the hash value computed on the fetched authorization matches the one received in the handshake. A mismatch of the hash values SHOULD be treated as though the authorization was not provided, which results in a bad_certificate alert.

Other schemes may also be supported, but circular dependencies MUST be avoided when dereferencing these URLs, and avoiding TLS when dereferencing them is one way to do that. A client using the HTTP scheme therefore MUST NOT use these TLS extensions if the Upgrade mechanism in HTTP is in use. For other schemes, similar care must be taken to avoid using these TLS extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: The second option sends a URL and a one-way hash instead of the credentials themselves. The receiver fetches the list from the URL and checks that the hash matches. A mismatch is treated as if no permission had been given at all.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered two new entries in the TLS Authorization Data Formats registry, which is defined in RFC 5878: keynote_assertion_list(64) and keynote_assertion_list_url(65).

Appendix A of the RFC shows an updated version of the relevant data structures from section 3.3 of RFC 5878 with the new entries added, marking the added lines with two asterisks. The AuthorizationDataEntry structure gains two cases, one carrying a KeyNoteAssertionList and one carrying a URLandHash, and the AuthzDataFormat enumeration gains the two new values alongside the existing X.509 attribute certificate and SAML assertion entries. The URLandHash structure holds a URL of up to 2^16-1 bytes, a hash algorithm chosen from md5, sha1, sha224, sha256, sha384 and sha512, and the matching hash.
sections.plainLanguage: Two new values were added to the TLS authorization data format registry, 64 and 65, one for each way of carrying KeyNote credentials. The RFC also shows the updated structures that refer to them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that there are no security considerations beyond those discussed in RFC 2704, which describes the KeyNote trust-management system, in RFC 2792, which describes the DSA and RSA key and signature encoding for that system, and in RFC 5878, which describes the TLS authorization extensions. The document adds nothing further of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no rules of its own. It says the security considerations are already covered by the KeyNote specification, the key encoding specification and the TLS authorization extension specification.
